modes.openingLine:
Oscar-worthy drama; excellent. Now enjoy the low-budget factual remake.

Give the worry the movie trailer it has clearly been auditioning for.
modes.ritualCard:
Give the worry the movie trailer it has clearly been auditioning for.
Describe the feared situation for 10 sec like a blockbuster trailer. Replay the exact same event like silent CCTV: who, where, what movement, what words.
Guess which version will feel more dangerous: the dramatic trailer or the boring CCTV cut.
Check if the body reacts differently even though the basic event stayed the same. Editing changed the emotional impact before reality changed at all.

modes.openingLine:
Your sentence just went through airport security. The drama liquids stayed behind.

Let’s see how much emotional weight is hiding inside descriptive words.
modes.ritualCard:
Let’s see how much emotional weight is hiding inside descriptive words.
Say the thought once. Now remove words like awful, humiliating, impossible, terrible, rude, disastrous, pathetic. Keep only nouns, verbs, times and places.
Guess whether the story will feel weaker, stronger, or identical after the adjectives disappear.
Listen to what survives when the emotional colouring is stripped out. Adjectives often smuggle a verdict into a description.

modes.openingLine:
Three camera crews, zero need to solve the mystery tonight.

You have one camera angle and your brain has already written everyone else’s dialogue.
modes.ritualCard:
You have one camera angle and your brain has already written everyone else’s dialogue.
Picture the situation from three impossible camera positions: behind the other person, five minutes before, and five minutes after. Give each angle one plausible detail you did not see.
Guess how many plausible explanations you can create without changing the visible facts.
Notice how easily the meaning changes when hidden context changes. The original interpretation was one camera angle, not the whole set.

modes.openingLine:
Three drawers. Much better than the old “OH NO” filing cabinet.

Your brain may have shoved “possible” into the “basically happening” drawer.
modes.ritualCard:
Your brain may have shoved “possible” into the “basically happening” drawer.
Say only what you can justify. If you cannot defend “likely,” move it to “possible.” If you cannot estimate it at all, move it to “unknown.”
Choose which drawer the thought belongs in before you inspect it: likely, possible, or unknown.
Notice how different “unknown” feels from “dangerous.” Uncertainty and threat are not synonyms, even when your nervous system files them together.

modes.predict: Choose which drawer the thought belongs in before you inspect it: likely, possible, or unknown.
modes.play: Say only what you can justify. If you cannot defend “likely,” move it to “possible.” If you cannot estimate it at all, move it to “unknown.”
modes.catch: Notice how different “unknown” feels from “dangerous.”
modes.reveal: Uncertainty and threat are not synonyms, even when your nervous system files them together.
modes.mindBend: Unknown is a gap in information, not automatic evidence of disaster.
modes.safety:
PAUSE
Keep the sentence to the imagined or uncertain part of the situation. If there is a concrete safety problem, respond to the real problem rather than reframing it. Stop at the planned endpoint rather than repeating the ritual until it feels completely convincing.
modes.targetPattern: Binary threat categorisation
modes.theoryBackbone: Probability calibration; intolerance of uncertainty; risk perception
modes.mechanismFingerprint: Force categorical separation of likelihood, mere possibility and unquantified uncertainty.

Check whether meaninglessness for sixty seconds actually damaged anything. The pressure to make every moment matter can become heavier than the moment itself.

Reality stayed seated while meaning changed outfits three times.

Same event. Three meanings. Let’s see which part is actually glued to reality.
modes.ritualCard:
Same event. Three meanings. Let’s see which part is actually glued to reality.
Give the event three interpretations: one harsh, one boring, one unexpectedly generous. Don’t decide which is true yet.
Guess whether you can make the event mean three different things without changing what happened.
Notice that the facts stayed still while the emotional meaning moved. Meaning is often constructed after the event, not delivered inside it.

Reality stayed seated while meaning changed outfits three times.

HOOK
Same event. Three meanings. Let’s see which part is actually glued to reality.

PREDICT
Guess whether you can make the event mean three different things without changing what happened.

PLAY
Give the event three interpretations: one harsh, one boring, one unexpectedly generous. Don’t decide which is true yet.

CATCH
Notice that the facts stayed still while the emotional meaning moved.

REVEAL
Meaning is often constructed after the event, not delivered inside it.

MIND BEND
Events happen once. Meaning can be edited more than once.

MOVE ON

Imagine this problem behind glass five years from now.

Notice what shrinks when the time horizon expands. Distance changes the size of details without claiming they are meaningless now.

modes.openingLine:
No audience, no confetti. What still survives?

Let’s check whether this goal is yours or merely renting space in your calendar.
modes.ritualCard:
Let’s check whether this goal is yours or merely renting space in your calendar.
Imagine quietly stopping. Who appears first in your mind looking disappointed, impressed, confused or relieved? Name them. Ask what you would still want if nobody ever found out.
Guess whose reaction matters most if you imagine quitting the goal tomorrow.
Notice the gap between the audience goal and the private goal. Approval can power a goal without making the goal personally meaningful.

Congratulations, the treadmill finally has an OFF button.

If “more” has no finish line, it can run forever.

If “more” has no finish line, it can run forever.
Pick the thing you are chasing. Name a concrete “enough for today” line: one task, one answer, one check, one amount, one hour. Imagine getting double. Would today genuinely improve twice as much?
Guess the exact point where more money, praise, checking, achievement or certainty would stop noticeably changing today.
Watch for diminishing returns hiding behind the word “more.” Without a stopping rule, desire keeps moving the goalpost after every win.

Finish five fragments: “I notice… I care about… I’m curious about… I tend to… I’m learning…” Avoid every role label.

Notice how much self remains when the résumé disappears. Roles organise life, but they are not the full inventory of a person.

Instead of asking “What feels safest now?”
modes.ritualCard:
Instead of asking “What feels safest now?”
Imagine tomorrow night. Play two ten-second endings: you took the smallest reasonable step, or you avoided it. Which ending leaves less residue?
Guess which future regret feels heavier: trying imperfectly or avoiding completely.
Check if fear and regret point in the same direction or different ones. Short-term relief and long-term alignment often vote differently.

Your air-conditioner just delivered a tiny philosophy lecture.

Choose one sound and wait for it to betray its own sameness.

Choose one sound and wait for it to betray its own sameness.

Catch the moment “constant” becomes obviously variable. Attention reveals micro-changes that a stressed brain compresses into “this is just how it is.”

modes.openingLine:
Three seconds of grumpy bulldog. Then release.

Make tension obvious on purpose so release has something to compare with.
modes.ritualCard:
Make tension obvious on purpose so release has something to compare with.
Gently clench your jaw for three seconds—no pain—then let it hang loose. Do nothing else.
Guess whether your jaw is already closer to “soft” or “clenched.”
Notice which state suddenly becomes easier to identify because you created contrast. The nervous system notices differences better than vague instructions to “relax.”

Three tiny cuts. Your inner film editor approves.

Your eyes have a built-in edit button.

Your eyes have a built-in edit button.
Blink slowly three times. Each time, notice the instant the visual world disappears and returns.

Catch the tiny “new frame” feeling after each reopening. Perception is stitched from interruptions, even when experience feels continuous.

modes.openingLine:
Tiny body edit. No full renovation required.

Change exactly one joint and see if the emotional weather notices.
modes.ritualCard:
Change exactly one joint and see if the emotional weather notices.
Freeze your current posture. Rate its tension from 0–10. Change one joint only—drop shoulders, uncurl hands, uncross ankles. Re-rate.
Guess whether moving only your shoulders, hands or jaw will change anything at all.
Look for even a one-point change without trying to “feel better.” Body configuration is one ingredient in state, not merely a passive result of it.

Do one ordinary movement at half speed and see whether the deadline explodes.
modes.ritualCard:
Do one ordinary movement at half speed and see whether the deadline explodes.
Pick a harmless action—put down a cup, type one short sentence, fold a tissue—and do it at deliberately half your normal speed.
Guess what will happen if your hands move slowly for fifteen seconds.
Check if urgency rises, falls, or simply complains while time keeps moving normally. The feeling of rush can persist even when slower behaviour causes no consequence.

modes.predict: Guess what will happen if your hands move slowly for fifteen seconds.
modes.play: Pick a harmless action—put down a cup, type one short sentence, fold a tissue—and do it at deliberately half your normal speed.
modes.catch: Check if urgency rises, falls, or simply complains while time keeps moving normally.
modes.reveal: The feeling of rush can persist even when slower behaviour causes no consequence.
modes.mindBend: Urgency is a sensation. A deadline is a fact. They sometimes travel separately.
modes.safety:
PAUSE
Use the chosen example as a test, not a verdict. Stop if you begin forcing the result or using it to ignore information that clearly needs action. A single pass can test the pattern; it does not need to settle it permanently.
modes.targetPattern: Subjective speed mistaken for objective deadline
modes.theoryBackbone: Behavioural pacing; urgency discrimination; inhibitory control
modes.mechanismFingerprint: Slow motor output below subjective urgency rate and observe mismatch with objective consequence.

modes.openingLine:
Tiny navigation exam. No GPS allowed.

Your brain thinks it knows the room.
modes.ritualCard:
Your brain thinks it knows the room.
Look around once. Close your eyes. Point to three objects one by one. Open your eyes and compare the angles.
Guess how accurately you can point to three objects with your eyes closed.
Notice even small errors between the internal map and the actual room. The brain confidently fills missing spatial detail all day long.

modes.openingLine:
Your lungs have apparently been employed this whole time.

For once, do not improve your breathing.
modes.ritualCard:
For once, do not improve your breathing.
For three breaths, make no effort to deepen, slow, count or perfect anything. Just notice the instant each next breath begins on its own.
Guess whether breathing will become unsafe, chaotic, or simply continue if you stop managing it for three breaths.
Catch the body initiating what you were tempted to supervise. Some regulation happens better when you stop turning it into a performance review.

modes.openingLine:
Five universes. Your phone remains annoyingly silent in all of them.

One slow reply, five possible universes.
modes.ritualCard:
One slow reply, five possible universes.
Spin through five reasons for the delay: busy, driving, asleep, forgot, battery, family, work, unsure what to say, anything plausible. Only one slot may be about you.
Guess how many non-personal explanations you can produce before your brain returns to “they’re upset with me.”
Notice how much certainty the personal explanation loses once alternatives occupy the wheel. A delayed reply contains very little information about motive.

modes.openingLine:
Apparently the public is not running a detailed audit of your shoes.

How closely are people really studying you?
modes.ritualCard:
How closely are people really studying you?
Think of the last stranger you saw. Without cheating, recall their shoes, hair, facial expression and one flaw. Count what you genuinely remember.
Guess how many details you remember about the last stranger you passed.
Compare that memory with how closely you imagine strangers are tracking your details. People are usually the centre of their own attention, just as you are of yours.

Guess which details you know both people would agree on versus details you only remember from your own angle.
Notice where memory ends and interpretation begins. Shared events do not guarantee shared recordings because memory is reconstructed, not replayed.

modes.predict: Guess which details you know both people would agree on versus details you only remember from your own angle.
modes.play: List three facts any camera would capture. List three remembered meanings—tone, intention, emphasis, “what they knew.” Mark which items another witness could honestly remember differently.
modes.catch: Notice where memory ends and interpretation begins.
modes.reveal: Shared events do not guarantee shared recordings because memory is reconstructed, not replayed.
modes.mindBend: Two sincere memories can disagree without either person owning a perfect recording.
modes.safety:
PAUSE
Keep the list on the interpretation, not the other person's rights or limits. A kinder explanation does not cancel a clear no, repeated harm or needed distance. The result is a working perspective, not proof that the opposite story is true.
modes.targetPattern: Assuming shared memory is identical
modes.mechanismFingerprint: Partition conflict memory into camera facts and perspective-dependent reconstructions to reduce memory absolutism.

Three outfits. Same suspicious little question.

Your loop may be changing outfits while asking the same thing.
modes.ritualCard:
Your loop may be changing outfits while asking the same thing.
Take the last three versions of the loop. Rewrite each as a question. Now shrink them until the common demand appears: “Can I be certain?”, “Why did this happen?”, “What if…?”, “Am I okay?”
Guess how many recent thoughts reduce to one repeated question.
Check if the content was moving while the question stayed parked. A loop can feel productive because the wording changes even when the mental job does not.

Tiny paper brain installed.

Give the unfinished thing somewhere physical to live besides your head.
modes.ritualCard:
Give the unfinished thing somewhere physical to live besides your head.
Write exactly one next physical action on a small piece of paper: “email Sam,” “open invoice,” “put form in bag.” Fold the paper and place it where you will see it later.
Guess whether your mind will keep rehearsing the task after the next action is captured externally.
Wait ten seconds and check whether the task feels equally necessary to rehearse. A captured next step can reduce the brain’s need to keep an unfinished intention active.

Your loop has been using prestige-drama pacing.

Your loop has been using prestige-drama pacing.
Replay the exact thought in your head at absurdly fast cartoon speed. No pausing for emotional emphasis. Run it through three times.
Guess whether the thought feels equally authoritative at ridiculous double speed.
Check if it becomes harder to treat each phrase like a solemn revelation. Processing style changes emotional weight even when the words are identical.

Put three numbers in the doorway and make the loop squeeze past them.

Set five seconds. Try hard not to think the target thought. The instant it appears, just notice that the ban itself kept checking for it.
Guess whether forcefully banning it will make it appear less or more.
Catch the monitoring process asking, “Am I thinking it yet?” Suppression requires searching for the thing you are trying to exclude.

Three loops entered. New information may have missed the train.

If this is problem solving, it should be producing something new.
modes.ritualCard:
If this is problem solving, it should be producing something new.
Replay the last three rounds mentally. For each, name one new fact, decision or action that did not exist before. If there is none, mark it “replay.”
Guess how many genuinely new facts appeared in the last three loops.
Notice the difference between thinking longer and learning more. Repetition can feel effortful without generating information.

Compress the whole loop until only seven words survive.

Notice what your brain considers essential once there is no room for courtroom speeches. Elaboration adds emotional fuel; compression can reveal the small core question underneath.

modes.openingLine:
Your wall has one new temporary tenant.

Your thought feels inside your head.
modes.ritualCard:
Your thought feels inside your head.
Point to a wall, chair or object and imagine the sentence printed there. Move your eyes to it, then away from it, then back.
Guess where in the room the thought would “sit” if it had to occupy a physical spot.
Check if the thought becomes something you can look toward rather than something you are inside. Spatialising mental content can create a simple sense of distance without denying the content.

Notice that the future task is objectively smaller without any future motivation being required. Environment can carry part of the behavioural load that we usually dump onto willpower.

Keep shrinking the task until resistance starts laughing.

Notice the exact size where “I can’t” becomes “well, obviously I can do that.” Resistance is sensitive to task size, not only task importance.

modes.openingLine:
Tiny work sprint, guaranteed escape hatch.

Start with the exit already guaranteed.
modes.ritualCard:
Start with the exit already guaranteed.
Set ninety seconds. Work on the task until the timer rings. At the bell, stop mid-progress on purpose. Leave one obvious next step visible.
Guess whether work feels safer when the timer—not completion—decides when you stop.
Check if starting felt easier when the session had a hard ending. A bounded work period reduces the hidden fear that starting means being trapped until completion.

modes.displayName: A OR B, C IS CLOSED
modes.openingLine:
Option C is on annual leave.

Temporarily close every option except two.
modes.ritualCard:
Temporarily close every option except two.
Pick the decision. Choose the two most reasonable options. For 60 sec, pretend every other option is unavailable. Decide only between A and B.
Guess whether losing options feels relieving or irritating.
Check if mental noise drops when comparison space shrinks. More choice can increase analysis cost even when it increases theoretical freedom.

Two hands, two truths, zero cage match.

Give each side a hand so neither has to shout over the other.

Give each side a hand so neither has to shout over the other.
Hold one palm up for the want and the other for the fear. Say one honest sentence to each hand. Don’t force a winner.

Check if the conflict feels different when both truths are allowed to exist at once. Ambivalence is not necessarily confusion; sometimes it is two valid systems reporting simultaneously.

modes.openingLine:
Two radio stations. We were accidentally mixing the signals.

Your brain may be answering “Will it happen?”
modes.ritualCard:
Your brain may be answering “Will it happen?”
Say both separately: “I predict ____ will happen.” Then: “I really Don’t want ____ to happen.” Rate each sentence from 0–10 for certainty/intensity.
Guess which sentence is actually stronger in you: the forecast or the preference.
Check if emotional intensity is being used as if it were probability evidence. Strong preference against an outcome can make the outcome feel more likely without adding predictive information.

modes.openingLine:
Fifteen seconds of body notes. Memoir postponed.

Give the body fifteen seconds before the autobiography begins.
modes.ritualCard:
Give the body fifteen seconds before the autobiography begins.
For fifteen seconds, describe only location, size, temperature, movement, pressure and rhythm of the feeling. Every “because” gets deleted.
Guess which explanation your mind will try to add first.
Catch how urgently the brain tries to convert sensation into a story about your life. Observation and explanation are separate mental acts, even when they arrive almost together.

Visitor sticker issued. No permanent office assigned.

Give the feeling a visitor badge instead of house ownership papers.
modes.ritualCard:
Give the feeling a visitor badge instead of house ownership papers.
Replace “I am [emotion]” with “[emotion] is here right now.” Imagine writing that emotion on a temporary visitor sticker, complete with today’s date.
Guess which feels more permanent: “I am anxious” or “anxiety is visiting right now.”
Notice any shift in permanence without asking the emotion to leave. Language can turn a current state into an identity claim before we notice the upgrade.

modes.openingLine:
One-minute guest pass. No need to redecorate for it.

For one minute, the feeling is allowed to stay without being fixed.
modes.ritualCard:
For one minute, the feeling is allowed to stay without being fixed.
Set 60 sec. Say: “You can be here until the timer ends.” Don’t feed the story, soothe, push away or measure every second. Just let the feeling occupy whatever space it already occupies.
Guess what will happen if you stop trying to reduce it for sixty seconds.
At the bell, notice what changed: intensity, location, texture, or only your struggle with it. Permission does not guarantee the feeling shrinks. It tests whether fighting it was adding a second layer.

modes.openingLine:
Tiny sentence. Surprisingly crowded backstage.

That conclusion may be standing on more invisible dominoes than it admits.
modes.ritualCard:
That conclusion may be standing on more invisible dominoes than it admits.
Say the conclusion. Keep asking, “What has to be true for that?” Write each answer as a separate domino until you reach something directly observed.
Guess how many separate things must be true before your conclusion can be true.
Count how many unverified dominoes sit between the observation and the conclusion. The conclusion felt like one thought, but it may depend on a whole chain of guesses.

modes.openingLine:
Maybe it was personality. Maybe Tuesday was just being Tuesday.

Did they reveal their personality—or did you catch them in weather?
modes.ritualCard:
Did they reveal their personality—or did you catch them in weather?
Take the behaviour you’re judging. First finish: “They did that because they are ___.” Then finish: “They did that because the situation was ___.” Use the same event.
Guess whether your explanation changes when the exact behaviour is done by someone you already like.
Notice which version felt automatic and which one required imagination. Person explanations arrive faster than situation explanations, especially when we’re annoyed.

modes.openingLine:
Fresh evidence smells stronger. That doesn’t make it the whole pantry.

Your brain is reviewing the whole season using the last scene.
modes.ritualCard:
Your brain is reviewing the whole season using the last scene.
Name the most recent event driving the feeling. Deliberately name three earlier events from the same category—good, bad, or neutral.
Guess whether your verdict changes when you sample from the last month instead of the last hour.
Compare your first verdict with the four-event sample. Recent information gets extra psychological weight simply because it is still warm.

VIBE: CHEEKY

Your last scene got promoted to executive producer.

HOOK
Your brain is reviewing the whole season using the last scene.

PREDICT
Guess whether your verdict changes when you sample from the last month instead of the last hour.

PLAY
Name the most recent event driving the feeling. Deliberately name three earlier events from the same category—good, bad, or neutral.

CATCH
Compare your first verdict with the four-event sample.

REVEAL
Recent information gets extra psychological weight simply because it is still warm.

MIND BEND
What happened last can matter without becoming what happens always.

MOVE ON
↻ LAST SCENE ≠ WHOLE SEASON

modes.openingLine:
Definitions: ruining dramatic labels since forever.

Let’s make your scary label pass a definition test.
modes.ritualCard:
Let’s make your scary label pass a definition test.
Write 1 line beginning, “For anything to count as failure, it must…” Make the rule concrete enough to use on someone else. Now test today’s event against it.
Guess whether your current event still qualifies as “failure” under a rule you would apply consistently.
Watch whether the label survives once its criteria stop moving around your mood. Vague labels can win arguments because they never have to meet a fixed threshold.
↻ WHAT COUNTS AS FAILURE?

modes.openingLine:
Your memory can sound HD while storing surprisingly few pixels.

Let’s separate how certain the memory feels from how much detail it actually carries.
modes.ritualCard:
Let’s separate how certain the memory feels from how much detail it actually carries.
Without embellishing, list concrete sensory details you can genuinely retrieve: exact words, location, sequence, colours, sounds. Put a question mark beside anything reconstructed.
Rate confidence in the memory from 0–100 before you inspect it.
Compare the confidence number with the amount of verifiable detail you could retrieve. Memory confidence and memory detail can travel on different tracks.

Red dot spotted. White page would like equal billing.

Your attention found the red dot.
modes.ritualCard:
Your attention found the red dot.
Now map the current situation the same way: name the one negative detail your mind keeps circling, then name three neutral or positive details that are also on the page.
Imagine a white page with one red dot. Guess which part your eyes would report first.
Check if the red detail became less true—or simply less alone. Threat-relevant details are designed to win attention, not to provide a balanced summary.

One tiny word may be doing most of the emotional damage.
modes.ritualCard:
One tiny word may be doing most of the emotional damage.
Say the thought once. Replace only the absolute word with the narrowest accurate alternative: “sometimes,” “this person,” “today,” “a few.” Don’t change anything else.
Guess which word changes the feeling more: the event itself, or “always / everyone / never / nothing.”
Listen for the emotional shift caused by a single grammatical change. Quantifiers quietly decide how large the problem is allowed to become.

Your brain loves matching patterns.

Your brain loves matching patterns.
Finish two lines: “This looks like ___ because ___.” Then: “How often does ___ happen in situations like this?” If you Don’t know, write UNKNOWN rather than guessing.
Guess whether your conclusion is based more on resemblance or on actual frequency.
Check if the pattern match had an answer while the frequency question did not. Resemblance is quick evidence for similarity, not automatic evidence for probability.

“Possible” covers everything from meteor strike to missed bus.

PREDICT
Ask: is your worry merely possible, reasonably plausible, or expected soon?

PLAY
Draw three imaginary boxes: POSSIBLE, PLAUSIBLE, EXPECTED. Put the feared event in one box based on the evidence you have—not on how unpleasant it would be.

CATCH
Check if your body had been reacting to the first box as though it were the third.

REVEAL
Possibility answers “can it happen?” It does not answer “how much should I expect it?”

MIND BEND
Possible is not a probability. It is a very large country.

MOVE ON
↻ POSSIBLE IS A HUGE COUNTRY

modes.openingLine:
Plot twist: your life may not be running on their timetable.

Whose clock is making that ticking noise?
modes.ritualCard:
Whose clock is making that ticking noise?
Name the milestone that feels late. Now imagine every comparison person disappears for a day. Ask: “Would this still need to happen by this exact age or date?”
Guess whether the deadline came from your values, your peers, your family, or the internet.
Check if urgency survives when the audience disappears. Some deadlines measure logistics. Others measure comparison.

modes.openingLine:
Secret achievement mode: surprisingly revealing.

Let’s make the goal invisible and see if you still want it.
modes.ritualCard:
Let’s make the goal invisible and see if you still want it.
Picture completing the goal perfectly—but no post, no praise, no title, no one finds out. Sit with that version for 10 sec.
Guess whether desire goes up, down, or stays the same if nobody will ever know you achieved it.
Notice what happens to the pull of the goal when visibility is removed. Recognition can be part of a goal without being the same thing as wanting the goal.
↻ THE INVISIBLE VERSION

modes.openingLine:
Admission free. Emotional gift shop optional.

Some goals deserve progress.
modes.ritualCard:
Some goals deserve progress.
Imagine the goal behind museum glass labelled: “Important to me from ____ to ____.” Now ask whether you want to take it home again—or simply respect that it mattered then.
Pick one stubborn goal. Guess whether you would choose it today if you had never started it.
Check if ending the goal feels less like failure when its past value is preserved. A goal can have been meaningful without needing to remain active forever.

modes.openingLine:
Power outage at the achievement casino.

Turn off every scoreboard for ten seconds.
modes.ritualCard:
Turn off every scoreboard for ten seconds.
Imagine all comparison numbers vanish for a week. Pick one activity you would still continue because of how it feels, what it builds, or whom it serves.
Guess which achievement still feels worth doing with no rank, likes, salary comparison, marks, or praise visible.
Notice which motivations survive the blackout. Scoreboards are useful for measurement, but terrible at explaining why something matters.

modes.openingLine:
Nice jacket. Still not your skin.

Take the role off for a minute.
modes.ritualCard:
Take the role off for a minute.
Picture your main role—parent, manager, partner, achiever, helper—as a jacket on a hanger. For 10 sec answer: “What is here before I put that jacket back on?”
Guess what part of you feels missing when the role is temporarily removed.
Check if a self remains even when the role is not being performed. Roles organise behaviour. They are not the entire person wearing them.

Would this still matter if it did not guarantee the ending?
modes.ritualCard:
Would this still matter if it did not guarantee the ending?
Finish: “I can choose ___, but I cannot guarantee ___.” Make both halves concrete for today.
Choose a valued direction—kindness, courage, learning, honesty. Guess whether it remains worth doing if the outcome is uncertain.
Notice which part belongs to your behaviour and which part belongs to the world. Values can guide action without controlling results.

modes.predict: Choose a valued direction—kindness, courage, learning, honesty. Guess whether it remains worth doing if the outcome is uncertain.
modes.play: Finish: “I can choose ___, but I cannot guarantee ___.” Make both halves concrete for today.
modes.catch: Notice which part belongs to your behaviour and which part belongs to the world.
modes.reveal: Values can guide action without controlling results.
modes.mindBend: Meaning is often in the direction you choose, not the outcome you can force.
modes.safety:
PAUSE
Let this pass create movement without forcing commitment. Stop before any step that is unsafe, irreversible or beyond what you intended to test. If the same pattern returns later, re-check the new context rather than copying today's answer.
modes.targetPattern: Choosing only values with guaranteed outcomes
modes.theoryBackbone: ACT values; locus of control; committed action
modes.mechanismFingerprint: Split a valued action from the external outcome it cannot guarantee and test whether the value still stands.

modes.openingLine:
No cape. Just a charged phone and a nicer tomorrow.

Some of life’s meaning is hiding in jobs nobody applauds.
modes.ritualCard:
Some of life’s meaning is hiding in jobs nobody applauds.
Choose one invisible act: refill something, send a check-in, put an item back, prep breakfast, charge a device, tidy one surface. Name who benefits—even if it is only future-you.
Guess which tiny maintenance act would make tomorrow slightly kinder.
Notice how meaning changes when you measure by service rather than drama. Maintenance rarely looks heroic because its success is often that nothing goes wrong.

Regret keeps showing you one direction.
modes.ritualCard:
Regret keeps showing you one direction.
Create two ten-second future scenes: “I tried and it was wrong for me,” then “I never tried and still wonder.” Don’t choose yet; just compare the emotional texture.
Guess which regret feels louder: doing the thing and disliking it, or never testing it at all.
Check if your mind had been simulating only one kind of regret. Avoidance often protects us from visible regret while hiding invisible regret.

Take the choice and append: “for the next 30 days” or another realistic review window. Imagine revisiting it then with new information.

Check if identity pressure falls when permanence is removed. Many decisions are revisable, but the mind upgrades them into identity declarations.

Let’s move one sound out of the starring role without making it stop.

Check if the loud sound changed—or whether your attention changed its rank. Sensory dominance is partly about volume and partly about where attention points.

See whether your first prediction matched the actual pattern. Sensation becomes more detailed when attention stops asking only “good or bad?”

Let’s remind your eyes that the world has depth.

Check if your visual field feels different after travelling through depth. Threat tends to compress attention around what feels immediate.

Sort three sounds only by distance: near, medium, far. Ignore whether you like them.
Guess whether you can find one sound closer than your body and one farther than the room.
Notice how the sound field expands when distance replaces meaning as the sorting rule. Changing the dimension you attend to changes the experience without changing the sounds.

Free special effects, courtesy of having two eyes.

Your visual world is already being edited live.
modes.ritualCard:
Your visual world is already being edited live.
Pick your thumb or a small object. Look with both eyes, then close left, open, close right. Notice the tiny jump against the background.
Guess whether closing one eye changes the position of a nearby object against the background.
See how stable the world feels even though the raw inputs disagree. Your brain quietly combines imperfect inputs into one usable scene.

Your mind can sprint while the second hand strolls.

Watch a clock, timer, or slow count of ten. Don’t stop thoughts. Simply tally each noticeable jump in topic with a finger.
Guess how many separate thought fragments can appear during ten actual seconds.
Compare mental speed with external time. Internal urgency can accelerate while the clock remains completely unimpressed.

modes.ritualCard:

Choose a safe nearby object. Make the prediction. Touch it for five seconds while describing only physical qualities—edges, pressure, temperature, texture—without “nice” or “bad.”
Guess whether an object will feel pleasant, rough, cold, soft or boring before touching it.
Compare the predicted feeling with the actual sensory details. Expectation arrives before sensation and can colour what comes next.

modes.openingLine:
Found: one microscopic plot twist.

We are not looking for peace.
modes.ritualCard:
We are not looking for peace.
For 20 sec, watch only for change—not improvement. A blink, swallow, sound, movement, or thought switch counts if the experience is different.
Guess whether there is any half-second today when the discomfort changes, dips, shifts location, or gets interrupted.
Catch the first moment that proves the state is not perfectly continuous. The nervous system can feel constant while actually changing in tiny increments.

Shrink the visual world to something absurdly small.

Guess whether a tiny patch contains more detail than you normally notice.
Notice what happened to the rest of the room while the patch became detailed. Attention can trade breadth for detail on purpose instead of being dragged there by worry.

modes.play: Pick a patch about the size of a fingernail on any safe object. Spend 10 sec finding three details inside only that patch: colour variation, edge, fibre, scratch, light.
modes.catch: Notice what happened to the rest of the room while the patch became detailed.
modes.reveal: Attention can trade breadth for detail on purpose instead of being dragged there by worry.
modes.mindBend: A tiny piece of reality can be larger than a whole thought when you actually look.
modes.safety:
PAUSE
Do the chosen example once and keep the result provisional. If the exercise increases distress or confusion, stop rather than trying harder. A single pass can test the pattern; it does not need to settle it permanently.
modes.targetPattern: Complex scenes maintaining cognitive load
modes.theoryBackbone: Focused attention; visual discrimination; attentional control
modes.mechanismFingerprint: Constrain visual attention to a fingernail-sized region and extract multiple micro-features to displace global internal load.

modes.openingLine:
The period has legal representation now.

A full stop has been accused of having an attitude.
modes.ritualCard:
A full stop has been accused of having an attitude.
Read the same short message three ways in your head: with a period, with an exclamation mark, and with no punctuation. Keep the words unchanged.
Guess how much the message’s tone changes if punctuation changes but every word stays identical.
Notice how much emotion your mind manufactures from marks the sender may use habitually. Digital tone is partly inferred from tiny formatting cues that are highly ambiguous.

Your phone screen may be clear.
Take the message bothering you. Imagine receiving it immediately after something that made you feel secure or amused. Read it again in that imagined state.
Guess whether the same message would sound different if you read it after good news.
Notice which words stay the same while the inferred tone shifts. Our state helps supply the emotional colour of ambiguous communication.

modes.openingLine:
Telepathy department closed. Words are still open.

Did you make a request—or assign them a mind-reading exam?
modes.ritualCard:
Did you make a request—or assign them a mind-reading exam?
Recall what you said. Remove tone, facial expression and shared history. Using only the literal words, write what a stranger would think you asked for.
Guess whether the other person could repeat your exact need from the words you actually used.
Compare that with what you hoped the person would understand. Hints feel obvious from inside the mind that created them.
↻ ASK OR TELEPATHY?

We’re putting a circle around what happened—not around the whole human.
Complete: “When they ___, the impact on me was ___.” Ban “selfish,” “toxic,” “lazy,” “bad,” and every other identity label.

Your brain has a close-up.
Imagine the scene from a ceiling camera. Include phones, traffic, tasks, conversations, hunger, deadlines—everything competing for everyone’s attention.

See whether your mistake still occupies the same percentage of the frame. The spotlight effect grows when we confuse our close-up with everyone else’s camera angle.

Your brain keeps moving the goalposts after praise arrives.
modes.ritualCard:
Your brain keeps moving the goalposts after praise arrives.
Take one genuine compliment. For 30 sec, ban these escape hatches: “they were being nice,” “anyone could do it,” “it was luck,” “it doesn’t count.” Let the statement remain unedited.
Guess what explanation your mind will use to dismiss the compliment before you read it again.
Notice the discomfort of evidence that does not fit the old self-story. Discounting praise protects an existing belief by disqualifying inconvenient data.

This loop has a job.
modes.ritualCard:
This loop has a job.
Ask one question: “If I had the perfect answer right now, what would I do differently in the next hour?” If the answer is “nothing,” mark the loop SOOTHE, not SOLVE.
Guess whether the loop is producing a decision—or trying to make an uncomfortable feeling disappear.
Check if the thinking is actually linked to action. Problem solving changes a next step. Rumination often changes only the feeling of unfinishedness.

modes.play: Ask one question: “If I had the perfect answer right now, what would I do differently in the next hour?” If the answer is “nothing,” mark the loop SOOTHE, not SOLVE.
modes.catch: Check if the thinking is actually linked to action.
modes.reveal: Problem solving changes a next step. Rumination often changes only the feeling of unfinishedness.
modes.mindBend: Not every thought that feels like work is doing problem-solving work.
modes.safety:
PAUSE
Keep the question brief and single-pass. Stop if repeating it makes the thought louder, more detailed or harder to leave. Stop at the planned endpoint rather than repeating the ritual until it feels completely convincing.
modes.targetPattern: Thinking used either to solve or to regulate emotion
modes.mechanismFingerprint: Use a counterfactual perfect-answer test to classify repetitive thinking by whether it would alter near-term behaviour.

We’re going to remove the thought without arguing with it.
Say the looping sentence. Repeat it, removing 1 word each time from the end until only the first word remains. Say nothing.
Guess which word feels hardest to delete.
Notice which part of the sentence carried the emotional charge and when the meaning collapsed. Thoughts feel whole, but their impact depends on a sequence of ordinary words.

VIBE: UNFILTERED

Your feelings are allowed to be a damn blend.

HOOK
Your mood may be a mix, not a single paint colour.

PREDICT
Guess whether one label is hiding a second emotion underneath it.

PLAY
Choose up to three emotion words and give each a rough percentage. They Don’t need to total perfectly at first; adjust until the mix feels close enough.

CATCH
Check if the dominant feeling changes when the smaller colours are allowed in.

REVEAL
Mixed emotions are common, but single labels can hide their structure.

MIND BEND
You can be 50% angry, 30% hurt and 20% relieved without being inconsistent.

MOVE ON

modes.catch: Check if the feeling becomes more useful when converted into direction.

modes.mindBend: The sting may be pointing toward a value, not issuing a verdict on your worth.
modes.safety:
PAUSE

modes.targetPattern: Envy treated only as ugliness rather than information
modes.theoryBackbone: Social comparison; values clarification; motivational emotion
modes.mechanismFingerprint: Translate envy from person-focused comparison into the underlying valued quality or condition.

modes.openingLine:
Applause machine unplugged.

Delete the congratulations.
modes.ritualCard:
Delete the congratulations.
Imagine both options lead to zero recognition: no post, no compliments, no impressive explanation. Which daily reality do you lean toward?
Guess whether your preferred option changes if nobody can praise it later.
Notice what survives when future applause is removed. Anticipated social reward can masquerade as personal preference.

modes.play: Imagine both options lead to zero recognition: no post, no compliments, no impressive explanation. Which daily reality do you lean toward?
modes.catch: Notice what survives when future applause is removed.
modes.reveal: Anticipated social reward can masquerade as personal preference.
modes.mindBend: A choice may become clearer when nobody gets to admire it.
modes.safety:
PAUSE
Keep the mental image on the interpretation, not the other person's rights or limits. A kinder explanation does not cancel a clear no, repeated harm or needed distance. Stop at the planned endpoint rather than repeating the ritual until it feels completely convincing.
modes.targetPattern: Choice distorted by anticipated praise
modes.theoryBackbone: Extrinsic motivation; preference construction; social reward
modes.mechanismFingerprint: Remove anticipated future praise from competing options while preserving lived consequences to isolate private preference.

modes.openingLine:

There is a rule in your head.
modes.ritualCard:
There is a rule in your head.
Finish: “A good person should ___.” Then add: “According to ___.” If the source is vague, write CULTURE / FAMILY / OLD ME / UNKNOWN.
Guess who originally taught, rewarded or modelled it.
Check if the rule feels different once authorship appears. Internalised rules often feel self-authored after their source is forgotten.

modes.openingLine:
Ordinary thing temporarily promoted to treasure.

Sometimes value becomes obvious only when you imagine the absence.
modes.ritualCard:
Sometimes value becomes obvious only when you imagine the absence.
Choose one person, routine, ability or place you take for granted. Imagine it unavailable for one week—not forever. Name the first ordinary moment that would feel different.
Guess what ordinary thing you would miss more than you currently appreciate.
Notice what the imagined absence reveals about present value. Familiarity can hide importance by making it ordinary.

Trophy has been asked to explain its job description.

The trophy may be standing in for something else.
modes.ritualCard:
The trophy may be standing in for something else.
Take the goal and ask “What do I believe this gives me?” three times. Example: promotion → respect → security → freedom.
Guess what feeling or life condition you expect the goal to deliver.
Check if the final answer suggests more than one route. Goals often become symbols for deeper needs.

Catch the fact that perception feels continuous despite repeated gaps. The brain stitches interruptions into a stable scene.

Your world goes dark repeatedly and you barely notice.

modes.catch: Notice how inevitability weakens when chronology is scrambled.
modes.reveal: Narrative order helps create a sense that one thing naturally led to another.
modes.mindBend: A fixed sequence can feel like fate simply because it is the version you keep replaying.
modes.safety:
PAUSE
Keep the chosen example separate from fact-finding. A vivid or faint memory is not, by itself, proof of what happened. A single pass can test the pattern; it does not need to settle it permanently.
modes.targetPattern: A memory feels inevitable because events are replayed in one fixed sequence
modes.mechanismFingerprint: Reorder three autobiographical event snapshots to disrupt causal inevitability generated by habitual chronology.

Choose one review question only: lesson, repair, next action, or information needed. Answer it once. When answered, say REVIEW CLOSED.
Guess what one useful output would justify reviewing the event at all.
Catch any new question trying to keep the shop open. Reflection becomes rumination when the process has no stopping rule.

Serious thought, deeply unserious exit word.

We’re changing the exit ramp.

We’re changing the exit ramp.
Say the loop once, but deliberately replace the last word with a neutral unrelated word like “window” or “spoon.” Then stop.

Notice the tiny disruption in automatic continuation. Sequences rely on expected endings to cue what comes next.

If “next step” contains three verbs, it is probably not one step.
Say the next step aloud. Split it every time you hear “and,” “then,” or an implied choice. Keep only the first physical movement.

Notice how small an executable next step actually is. Tasks become heavy when decision bundles masquerade as single steps.

Silent audience, tiny activation boost.

Some tasks start easier when another human exists nearby.

Some tasks start easier when another human exists nearby.
Imagine a trusted person sitting nearby for 60 sec, or use a real body-doubling setup if available. Your only job is to begin one visible action.
Guess whether you would begin faster if someone silently watched you start.
Check if imagined or actual co-presence changes activation. Human presence can alter arousal and task engagement even without help.

Move one benign helpful object into easy view: water bottle, book, walking shoes, fruit, notebook. Change nothing else.
Guess which helpful action would happen more if its cue were visible.
Notice how visibility changes the number of moments the behaviour gets remembered. What is visible gets more opportunities to compete for action.

Your emotion may be guarding something specific.
modes.ritualCard:
Your emotion may be guarding something specific.
Name the emotion. Finish: “If this feeling could protect one thing, it would protect ___.” Don’t turn it into a command for someone else.
Guess what matters underneath the feeling: safety, respect, belonging, fairness, rest, competence, autonomy.
Check if the feeling becomes information about a value or need. Emotions often organise attention around what seems threatened or important.

Name the weather: angry, scared, flat, hurt. Name one compass action under 30 sec: pause, tell truth, leave kindly, ask, drink water, finish one step.
Guess one tiny action that would fit your values even if the feeling stays exactly the same.
Notice that direction does not require a different emotional climate first. Values can guide behaviour while emotion remains unresolved.

modes.openingLine:
Future spoilers removed from past-you’s exam.

Current-you has evidence past-you did not have.
modes.ritualCard:
Current-you has evidence past-you did not have.
Pick the old feeling. List what was known then, what was uncertain then, and what only became clear later. Judge the reaction using the first two columns only.
Guess whether you are judging an old reaction using today’s calmer knowledge.
Check if shame softens when hindsight evidence is removed. Emotions arise from the appraisal available at the time, not from future information.

modes.openingLine:
The missing bottom number has entered the chat.

Three bad moments sounds enormous until we ask: three out of how many?
modes.ritualCard:
Three bad moments sounds enormous until we ask: three out of how many?
Write the scary count on top: 3, 5, 10—whatever it is. Under it, estimate the total opportunities it came from. Turn it into “3 out of 40,” not just “3.”
Guess the total number of comparable moments in the same period.
Check if the numerator shrinks emotionally when its denominator appears. Counts feel bigger when the background population is invisible.

Your dramatic datapoint has been asked to sit with the class.

Your worst day applied to become your permanent trend line.
modes.ritualCard:
Your worst day applied to become your permanent trend line.
Pick one unusually bad or unusually good recent day. Now list three more ordinary examples from the same area before or after it.
Guess whether the next few similar days are likely to be equally extreme, worse, or closer to normal.
Compare the extreme point with the little cluster around it. Extreme observations are often followed by less extreme ones even when nobody fixes anything.

modes.displayName: WHAT ARE YOU BUYING WITH THE NO?

Receipt says: one no purchased three hours.

Every no spends something and buys something.
modes.ritualCard:
Every no spends something and buys something.
Take one thing you may decline. Write two columns: “I lose…” and “I buy…” Include time, energy, focus, peace, money, opportunity, identity, connection.
Guess what your refusal creates room for.
Check if the no still feels like pure loss once the purchased space is visible. Declining one option reallocates scarce resources to another.

Identity certificate printer has jammed.

Your brain saw one action and started issuing identity certificates.
modes.ritualCard:
Your brain saw one action and started issuing identity certificates.
Take the action you are using to define yourself. Imagine a stranger did it once. List three possible explanations besides fixed character.
Guess how much one behaviour should count as evidence about a whole person.
Notice how much more flexible the interpretation becomes when the person is not you. Actions can signal tendencies, but single acts are noisy measurements.

VIBE: UNFILTERED

Stop notarising your whole damn identity from one damn move.

HOOK
Your brain saw one action and started issuing identity certificates.

PREDICT
Guess how much one behaviour should count as evidence about a whole person.

PLAY
Take the action you are using to define yourself. Imagine a stranger did it once. List three possible explanations besides fixed character.

CATCH
Notice how much more flexible the interpretation becomes when the person is not you.

REVEAL
Actions can signal tendencies, but single acts are noisy measurements.

MIND BEND
One behaviour is evidence. It is not a full identity scan.

MOVE ON
↻ ONE ACTION, WEAK SIGNAL

Room empty. Opinions suddenly easier to hear.

Take the group out of the room and see what remains.
modes.ritualCard:
Take the group out of the room and see what remains.
Imagine making the decision in a world where friends, family and colleagues will never know the answer. What do you choose there?

Your visual system just muted a perfectly real thing.

Your eyes are about to prove they stop reporting things that stay still.
modes.ritualCard:
Your eyes are about to prove they stop reporting things that stay still.
Pick a harmless stationary edge or small mark. Look just beside it without moving your eyes much. Notice whether the edge fades, blurs, or becomes less prominent.
Guess whether a fixed edge stays equally vivid when you stare beside it for ten seconds.
Catch the moment the unchanging thing becomes less available. Sensory systems prioritise change over perfect continuous reporting.

Notice how comparison reveals effort that felt invisible alone. The nervous system notices contrast better than baseline.

modes.openingLine:
Silence had tiny tenants.

Silence is rarely empty.
modes.ritualCard:
Silence is rarely empty.
Listen for 10 sec, repeatedly choosing a quieter sound than the last one: hum, fabric, distant traffic, breath, electronics, room tone.
Guess whether you can find a sound quieter than the one you currently call background.
Notice how “silence” gains layers when attention changes resolution. Perception depends on what threshold attention is using.
↻ FIND THE QUIETEST NOISE

modes.openingLine:
Your eyeballs took the scenic route.

Let your eyes move before your thought does.
modes.ritualCard:
Let your eyes move before your thought does.
Keep your head mostly still. Slowly move your gaze from the far left of the room to the far right and back once, noticing objects you cross.
Guess whether slow horizontal eye movement changes the feeling of being mentally stuck.
Check if the mental scene feels equally narrow afterward. Visual exploration and attentional breadth are linked.
↻ HORIZON SWEEP

modes.openingLine:
Breathing refused to copy-paste.

Your last breath is trying to predict the next one.
modes.ritualCard:
Your last breath is trying to predict the next one.
Observe three natural breaths without changing them. Note one tiny difference in each: length, depth, pause, route, chest/belly movement.
Guess whether the next three breaths will be identical in depth and speed.
See whether the body repeats itself less exactly than expected. Biological rhythms vary from cycle to cycle.

modes.openingLine:
The calm room just acquired inner lives.

A calm-looking room can contain a lot of private panic.
modes.ritualCard:
A calm-looking room can contain a lot of private panic.
Picture the room. For three people, add one hidden internal possibility that would not show on their face: uncertainty, boredom, self-consciousness, tiredness, wanting to leave.
Guess how many people in a social situation might also be managing nerves invisibly.
Check if you still look uniquely uncomfortable. We compare our private experience with other people’s public surface.

Check if the single imbalance remains representative. Healthy reciprocity often balances over time rather than transaction by transaction.

Your face is not running closed captions.

modes.play: Take one repeated request from you or them. Imagine the literal request is impossible. Ask what emotional outcome the person may still be trying to get.
modes.catch: Check if the conflict changes when the hidden goal becomes visible.
modes.reveal: People often argue over the vehicle when the destination is the real issue.
modes.mindBend: A request can fail while the need beneath it remains understandable.
modes.safety:
PAUSE
Use the example you picked to reduce mind-reading, not to manufacture reassurance. Direct communication and boundaries carry more weight than guessed motives. The result is a working perspective, not proof that the opposite story is true.
modes.targetPattern: Surface request hiding a different relational need
modes.theoryBackbone: Needs-based communication; goal inference; interpersonal conflict
modes.mechanismFingerprint: Remove the literal requested behaviour and infer the relational outcome the request is attempting to produce.

modes.openingLine:

modes.ritualCard:
Ten people agreeing may contain fewer than ten independent judgments.
Take the crowd signal bothering you. Imagine person 2 saw person 1, person 3 saw the first two, and so on. Ask how many truly independent data points might remain.
Guess how many of the opinions could have been influenced by earlier opinions.
Notice how consensus strength changes when influence between people is allowed. Agreement is weaker evidence when opinions are socially linked.

Notice the strange jolt when linguistic momentum breaks. Language has continuation pressure independent of the truth of what it is saying.

Your brain may be open after the thinking department has closed.
modes.ritualCard:
Your brain may be open after the thinking department has closed.
Choose one recurring low-quality window. Make a rule: “No life verdicts in this state; only notes for tomorrow.”
Guess when your reasoning usually gets repetitive: late, hungry, exhausted, after conflict, after long work.
Notice how different the loop feels when it loses decision authority. Cognitive fatigue can increase repetition while reducing flexibility.

modes.openingLine:
Emotional instalment plan cancelled.

Your mind is trying to suffer early in case suffering later becomes cheaper.
modes.ritualCard:
Your mind is trying to suffer early in case suffering later becomes cheaper.
Imagine paying one emotional dollar every time you rehearse the feared outcome. Ask what concrete future benefit that payment buys.
Guess whether rehearsing the bad outcome actually reduces its probability or future pain.
Notice if the answer is only “I might feel prepared.” Anticipatory suffering often creates real cost without purchasing control.

modes.openingLine:
Notification received. Job offer declined.

A thought showed up.
modes.ritualCard:
A thought showed up.
Name the demanded job. Ask: “Who assigned this, and what happens if I Don’t accept it for ten minutes?”
Guess what action the thought is implicitly demanding: solve, check, confess, decide, replay, explain.
Notice the gap between mental appearance and behavioural obligation. Thoughts can generate task-like pressure without external requirements.

Check if the answer changes when sunk effort loses voting rights. Past costs cannot be recovered by spending more.

modes.predict: Guess which task you would choose if “importance” were banned and only “next” mattered.
modes.play: Look at your list. Ask not “What is most important?” but “What can physically happen next?” Pick 1 action with a verb and location.
modes.catch: Check if the priority debate shrinks when time becomes concrete.
modes.reveal: Global importance is abstract; next actions compete in real time.
modes.mindBend: You do not need one true priority for life. You need one next move.
modes.safety:
PAUSE
Keep the visual check within an ordinary safe task. A micro-step should reduce friction, not bypass limits, needed rest or a high-stakes decision process. Leave room for new evidence after the exercise instead of treating the result as final.
modes.targetPattern: Many important tasks making none behaviourally dominant
modes.theoryBackbone: Priority setting; action selection; temporal construal
modes.mechanismFingerprint: Replace global importance ranking with selection of one physically executable action for the immediate five-minute window.

modes.predict: Guess which looks more random: H-T-H-T-H-T or H-H-H-T-T-H.
modes.play: Imagine six coin tosses. Notice which sequence feels more random. Now remember that real randomness naturally produces runs, clumps and ugly streaks.
modes.catch: Catch the discomfort when random does not look evenly mixed.
modes.reveal: We expect randomness to look more balanced than randomness actually looks.
modes.mindBend: A streak can be real without being a signal.
modes.safety:
PAUSE
Keep the mental image light and reversible. The exercise should widen perspective, not pressure you to deny facts or push through rising distress. The result is a working perspective, not proof that the opposite story is true.
modes.targetPattern: Random streaks mistaken for hidden pattern

The last five outcomes are staring at the next one like they have influence.

Check if the feeling of 'tails is due' survives the empty table. Independent events do not repay imbalance on schedule.

modes.play: Identify the event that originally convinced you. Imagine learning tomorrow that this event was misunderstood or unreliable. What evidence remains?
modes.catch: Check if the belief stays at full strength after its foundation is removed.
modes.reveal: Beliefs can outlive the evidence that created them.
modes.mindBend: A conclusion does not inherit eternal life from its first proof.
modes.safety:
PAUSE
Keep this pass light and reversible. The exercise should widen perspective, not pressure you to deny facts or push through rising distress. Leave room for new evidence after the exercise instead of treating the result as final.
modes.targetPattern: A belief surviving after its original evidence disappears
modes.mechanismFingerprint: Counterfactually invalidate the original belief-forming evidence and reassess residual support from independent evidence.

modes.openingLine:
Same soup, different menu description.

Sometimes the label arrives before the experience and tells you what to feel.
modes.ritualCard:
Sometimes the label arrives before the experience and tells you what to feel.
Take a neutral experience: fast heartbeat, quiet room, difficult task. Give it two labels: 'danger' versus 'energy,' 'lonely' versus 'alone,' 'failure' versus 'draft.'
Guess how the same sensation sounds under two different labels.
Notice how interpretation shifts while the raw event stays still. Labels organise attention and meaning.
↻ SAME THING, NEW NAME

modes.displayName: WHAT NEED IS THIS GOAL FEEDING?
modes.openingLine:
Goal inspected. Hunger located.

Two identical goals can be feeding completely different hungers.
modes.ritualCard:
Two identical goals can be feeding completely different hungers.
Imagine achieving the goal but not receiving the need you named. Does the goal still satisfy?
Guess which need sits underneath this goal: autonomy, competence, connection, safety, status, novelty, rest.
Check if the goal itself or the need behind it has more emotional weight. Goals are vehicles; needs are often the destination.

modes.displayName: THE PLOT CAN HAVE LOOSE ENDS
modes.openingLine:
Plot department has approved one unexplained scene.

Your life is allowed to contain scenes that never become foreshadowing.
modes.ritualCard:
Your life is allowed to contain scenes that never become foreshadowing.
Name the event. For 10 sec, allow it to be 'something that happened' without deciding what it means for your destiny, identity, or future.
Guess which past event you keep trying to force into a neat story.
Notice the pressure created by leaving it narratively unfinished. Humans prefer coherent stories, even when life supplies messy fragments.

modes.displayName: WHICH ONE MOVED: YOU OR THE STORY?
modes.openingLine:
Choice made. PR department apparently arrived later.

Sometimes the choice happens first and the explanation gets hired afterward.
modes.ritualCard:
Sometimes the choice happens first and the explanation gets hired afterward.
Take a past choice between two decent options. Recall what you liked about the rejected one before deciding, then what you said about it after.
Guess whether your opinion of a rejected option became harsher after you chose against it.
Check if the option changed—or your story about it did. We often reduce discomfort by upgrading our choice and downgrading what we left.

modes.displayName: YOUR EYES JUMP, THE WORLD DOESN’T
modes.openingLine:
Your visual editor deleted the jump cut.

Your eyes make jumps all day.
modes.ritualCard:
Your eyes make jumps all day.
Use a mirror. Look at your left eye, then your right, switching back and forth. Try to catch the movement itself.
Guess whether you can see your own eyes moving in a mirror when you jump gaze from one eye to the other.
Notice you see the start and end positions but not the blur in between. The visual system suppresses parts of the signal during rapid eye movements.

Your eye has a blind spot.
modes.ritualCard:
Your eye has a blind spot.
Cover your left eye. Hold your right thumb out and fix your right eye on a small stationary object slightly to the left of the thumb. Slowly move the thumb sideways until it disappears.
Guess whether a small target can disappear while your eye remains open.
Catch the moment open-eye vision contains a missing object. The brain fills missing visual information so smoothly that the gap usually feels nonexistent.

modes.safety:

We are compressing the thought until the language loses its costume.
Write the first letter of each word in the looping sentence, separated by spaces. Read the code once.

Notice what remains when your brain has to reconstruct the sentence instead of receiving it fluently. Meaning feels immediate partly because language arrives already assembled.

modes.openingLine:
Inner narrator just became a podcast guest.

The voice in your head changes category when it comes out of a speaker.
modes.ritualCard:
The voice in your head changes category when it comes out of a speaker.
Record one ten-second voice memo saying the loop exactly once. Play it back once as if it came from a stranger. Stop.
Guess whether your loop sounds wiser, harsher, stranger, or more ordinary when recorded.
Notice what changes when the thought becomes an external sound object. Self-generated inner speech feels fused because it is experienced from inside production.

modes.openingLine:
Loop found to contain ad breaks.

modes.ritualCard:
The loop feels continuous.
Scan backward through your day until you find one interruption: shower, call, task, joke, driving turn, meal, message. Name what occupied the gap.
Guess the most recent moment today when you were not thinking about it, even briefly.
Notice that the loop had off-air moments even if it returned. Repeated thoughts can feel continuous because returns are remembered more than gaps.

Returning again does not mean the damn thing was there every damn second.

The loop feels continuous.
modes.ritualCard:
The loop feels continuous.
Scan backward through your day until you find one interruption: shower, call, task, joke, driving turn, meal, message. Name what occupied the gap.
Guess the most recent moment today when you were not thinking about it, even briefly.
Notice that the loop had off-air moments even if it returned. Repeated thoughts can feel continuous because returns are remembered more than gaps.

modes.openingLine:
Finish line just sent directions backward.

Forward planning loves discovering problems at the worst possible time.
modes.ritualCard:
Forward planning loves discovering problems at the worst possible time.
Picture the task complete. Ask what had to happen right before that, then what had to happen before that. Walk backward three steps.
Guess the step that must happen immediately before 'done.'
Notice which dependency becomes obvious from the finish line. Backward planning can expose prerequisites that forward momentum misses.

modes.displayName: LOCK IN BEFORE THE MOOD ARRIVES
modes.openingLine:
Future negotiation room has fewer chairs.

Decide while the persuasive future mood is not in the room.
modes.ritualCard:
Decide while the persuasive future mood is not in the room.
Choose one reversible commitment now: book the slot, prepare the food, block the site, place the item, tell someone the time, set the alarm. Make later avoidance slightly harder.
Guess which choice future-you is most likely to bargain away.
Notice the difference between deciding in a calm state and renegotiating inside temptation. Precommitment changes the choice environment before preference shifts.
↻ LOCK IN BEFORE THE MOOD ARRIVES

modes.openingLine:
Task has been issued walls and a closing time.

The task is trying to occupy the whole day because nobody gave it walls.
modes.ritualCard:
The task is trying to occupy the whole day because nobody gave it walls.
Choose a start time and stop time first. Make the box smaller than your fear of the task. Work only inside that box.
Guess how long you can work usefully before quality drops.
Check if a bounded container changes resistance. Open-ended effort is hard to price; bounded effort is easier to choose.

modes.openingLine:
Task has been moved into a smaller suitcase.

A giant time window can turn a small task into fog.
modes.ritualCard:
A giant time window can turn a small task into fog.
Take a routine task you know reasonably well. Give it a realistic but tighter window—about half the casual buffer, not half the necessary work.
Guess what would happen if you had half as long as usual.
Notice which low-value behaviours disappear first. Available time shapes how much process accumulates around a task.

modes.play: Take a claim from an expert or authority. Mentally delete the name, title, brand, uniform, or follower count. Read only the reasoning and evidence.
modes.catch: Notice what remains persuasive after status disappears.
modes.reveal: Authority can be useful evidence of expertise, but it can also replace inspection.
modes.mindBend: A title can strengthen a claim without becoming the claim.
modes.safety:
PAUSE
Do the example you picked once and keep the result provisional. If the exercise increases distress or confusion, stop rather than trying harder. Keep the result tied to this one example rather than generalising it to every situation.
modes.targetPattern: Expert status substituting for argument quality
modes.theoryBackbone: Authority bias; source credibility; argument evaluation
modes.mechanismFingerprint: Temporarily strip status cues from a claim and evaluate its reasoning before reintroducing source expertise.

modes.openingLine:

If you like something, your brain may quietly lower its risks too.
modes.ritualCard:
If you like something, your brain may quietly lower its risks too.
Take one choice. Rate BENEFIT and RISK separately before writing whether you personally like it.
Guess how your risk estimate changes when you imagine liking versus disliking the same option.
Check if the two numbers had been moving together simply because your feeling was global. Overall affect can substitute for separate analysis of costs and benefits.

When good outcomes are common, almost anything nearby can look responsible.
modes.ritualCard:
When good outcomes are common, almost anything nearby can look responsible.

Guess how often the good outcome happens even without the supposed cause.
Check if the cause still deserves all the credit. When outcomes happen frequently, coincidence can masquerade as effectiveness.

modes.openingLine:
Your search filter has been caught preloading results.

Once you expect something, your attention starts collecting supporting crumbs.
modes.ritualCard:
Once you expect something, your attention starts collecting supporting crumbs.
Take one ambiguous interaction. Scan it twice in memory: once looking only for signs of rejection, once looking only for signs of goodwill.
Guess what cue you would notice first if you expected rudeness versus kindness.
Notice how both searches can find material. Expectations guide what evidence gets sampled.

modes.openingLine:
Exclusive weirdness club has lost its exclusivity.

Your embarrassing reaction may be far less exclusive than your brain claims.
modes.ritualCard:
Your embarrassing reaction may be far less exclusive than your brain claims.
Imagine ten people in the same situation. Give at least three of them plausible internal reactions similar to yours, even if they hide them differently.
Guess what percentage of ordinary people would have some version of the same reaction.
Check if the feeling becomes less like evidence of personal defect. We often underestimate how common our uncomfortable traits and reactions are.

You may be treating a costume fitting like a wedding.
modes.ritualCard:
You may be treating a costume fitting like a wedding.
Take the identity claim—leader, artist, entrepreneur, introvert, athlete, caregiver. Design one small behaviour that lets you sample it for a week.
Guess what version of this identity you could test without committing to the label.
Check if curiosity appears when permanence disappears. Identity can be explored through behaviour before it is declared.

Imagine three chairs: past-you asks for compassion, current-you asks for something manageable, future-you asks for one favour. Give each 1 line.
Guess which version of you is currently being ignored.
Check if the decision changes when all three get representation. Self-continuity improves when different temporal selves are treated as connected stakeholders.

Choose one controllable handicap—late start, no preparation, distraction, impossible standard. Remove just that one for the next attempt.
Guess which obstacle you sometimes leave in place so failure has somewhere else to land.

modes.openingLine:
Two good things have been caught fighting over one calendar slot.

Sometimes you are stuck because both sides matter, not because you lack courage.
modes.ritualCard:
Sometimes you are stuck because both sides matter, not because you lack courage.
Name both without making either stupid: freedom vs security, honesty vs kindness, ambition vs rest, loyalty vs growth.
Guess which two values are pulling against each other.
Notice how the conflict changes when both sides are respected. Hard choices often involve competing goods rather than good versus bad.

An old insult can feel more believable than a new compliment simply because it matches the file.

An old insult can feel more believable than a new compliment simply because it matches the file.
Choose one positive piece of feedback that clashes with your self-story and one negative piece that fits it. Notice which one your mind cross-examines harder.
Guess which feedback your brain accepts faster: familiar criticism or unfamiliar praise.
Catch the unequal evidence standard. People often prefer information that confirms a stable self-view, even when the view is unkind.

Your eyes can keep a colour after the object is gone.
modes.ritualCard:
Your eyes can keep a colour after the object is gone.
Look at a non-bright coloured object for about fifteen seconds, then shift to a plain white or light wall. Don’t use lights or the sun.
Guess what colour ghost appears after staring at one safe coloured object.
Catch the faint complementary colour that may appear. Visual receptors adapt, and the contrast system keeps processing after the stimulus leaves.

Catch the mismatch between appearance and ruler. Surrounding geometry changes perceived length.

modes.play: Do one ten-second interval tracking three small changes around you. One ten-second interval on a single still point. Use the same clock.
modes.catch: Compare subjective length with identical clock time.
modes.reveal: Event density influences experienced duration.
modes.mindBend: Time on the clock can stay fixed while time in experience stretches.
modes.safety:
PAUSE
Let this pass change the story around the feeling without invalidating the feeling itself. If distress rises sharply, stop rather than push through. A single pass can test the pattern; it does not need to settle it permanently.
modes.targetPattern: Busy intervals feeling longer in the moment than empty ones
modes.theoryBackbone: Time perception; event density; prospective duration
modes.mechanismFingerprint: Compare equal timed intervals containing high versus low event density and observe differences in subjective duration.

modes.openingLine:
Same luggage, better packing cubes.

Memory size changes when the pieces learn to travel together.
modes.ritualCard:
Memory size changes when the pieces learn to travel together.
Take a long sequence of digits or letters. Read it once as separate items, then reorganise it into meaningful or rhythmic chunks.
Guess which is easier: remembering 2-0-2-6-0-9-1-8-4-2 or 2026 / 0918 / 42.
Notice how the same information occupies fewer mental slots. Working memory capacity depends partly on how information is grouped.

Calm-you is very confident about what upset-you should do.

Calm-you is very confident about what upset-you should do.
Choose one state. Write what calm-you expects. Remember a real moment inside that state and what felt important then.
Guess whether your rules for yourself change when hungry, angry, lonely, excited, or exhausted.
Notice the gap between advice from outside the state and priorities inside it. People mispredict behaviour across different emotional and physiological states.

Notice how certainty changes when individual variation returns. Group-level patterns do not determine individual outcomes.

One vivid person can hit harder than a huge anonymous group.

One vivid person can hit harder than a huge anonymous group.

Catch where emotion stops scaling with quantity. Human empathy is more responsive to identifiable individuals than large numbers.

Drawer organisation has been called in for questioning.

Sometimes chaos in one area makes you crave control in a totally different drawer.
modes.ritualCard:
Sometimes chaos in one area makes you crave control in a totally different drawer.
Name one uncontrollable disruption and one area where you have suddenly become extra rule-bound, tidy, strict, or certain.
Guess whether a recent uncertainty is making you unusually rigid somewhere else.
