modes.openingLine:
Scene changed. Attention was apparently on annual leave.

Your eyes can miss a big change if the scene gets interrupted at the right moment.
modes.ritualCard:
Your eyes can miss a big change if the scene gets interrupted at the right moment.
Arrange three harmless objects. Look away, move one slightly, then look back. If someone can help, let them do the move while you turn.
Guess whether you would notice an object moved if you looked away briefly.
Catch how attention, not just vision, determines change detection. Seeing a scene does not mean every feature is continuously represented.

Ask someone to read a quick stream of letters with two numbers embedded close together, or simulate by rapidly scanning a short mixed sequence. Notice whether the second target is harder.
Guess whether two important items are equally easy to notice when they arrive almost back-to-back.
Catch the tiny recovery period after the first target grabs attention. Attention has a brief processing bottleneck.

modes.openingLine:
Reading barged into a colour task uninvited.

Your brain reads before you ask it to.
modes.ritualCard:
Your brain reads before you ask it to.
Write colour words in mismatched pen colours. Name the ink colours, not the words.
Guess how much slower it feels to name the ink colour of the word RED printed in blue.
Notice the tug of the automatic reading response. Automatic processes can interfere with intentional ones.

modes.openingLine:
Eyes have apparently joined the audio department.

What you see can change what you think you heard.
modes.ritualCard:
What you see can change what you think you heard.
Watch a muted person's mouth forming one syllable while imagining a different sound, or use any familiar example where lip shape conflicts with expected speech. Notice the pull.
Guess whether mouth movement could alter an ambiguous spoken syllable.
Catch how vision participates in hearing speech. Speech perception integrates multiple senses.

Your brain likes sound to come from where the action looks like it is happening.
modes.ritualCard:
Your brain likes sound to come from where the action looks like it is happening.
Play a safe audio source while looking at a visible object or screen that appears to 'speak.' Notice where the sound seems to belong.
Guess whether a voice feels located closer to a moving face than to the actual speaker.
Catch the location shift created by visual capture. Vision often dominates sound localisation.

modes.mindBend: The sound did not change categories; your brain changed the grouping.

A sentence can become smoother simply because you have heard it many times.

A sentence can become smoother simply because you have heard it many times.
Say a harmless false sentence several times, like 'bananas grow on pine trees.' Notice how familiarity rises even while truth stays false.
Guess whether the thought feels more believable after the tenth repetition than the first.
Catch fluency increasing without evidence. Repeated exposure increases processing fluency, which can be mistaken for truth.

Notice the memory's edit history. Recall is reconstructive and can alter later memory.

modes.displayName: CLOSE THE LOOP WITH A PLACEHOLDER
modes.openingLine:
Unfinished task has been given a bookmark instead of haunting rights.

Your brain may keep the task open because it cannot see where it resumes.
modes.ritualCard:
Your brain may keep the task open because it cannot see where it resumes.
For an unfinished task, write: 'Stopped at ___; restart with ___.' Then deliberately stop.
Guess whether one clear restart marker reduces intrusive task reminders.
Check if unfinishedness feels more contained. Unfinished goals stay cognitively accessible, especially when next steps are unclear.

Take the urge to act. List what waiting preserves or reveals: response, price, emotion cooling, more data, other person's action.
Guess what information would arrive naturally if you waited one hour or one day.
Check if action was solving the problem or solving your discomfort with waiting. People often prefer action because inaction feels passive and aversive.

Your favourite coping move may be brilliant in one situation and useless in another.
modes.ritualCard:
Your favourite coping move may be brilliant in one situation and useless in another.
Take the current emotion. Ask what job it needs: change situation, reduce arousal, understand need, wait, connect, act.
Guess which strategy you reach for automatically: distract, talk, analyse, rest, act, breathe, avoid, solve.
Check if your default strategy matches the job. Emotion regulation works through strategy–context fit.

Nearby emotion words can point to very different action sizes.

Nearby emotion words can point to very different action sizes.

Guess which fits better: annoyed, irritated, angry, furious.
Check if the action urge shrinks when the label becomes proportionate. Emotion intensity categories influence appraisal and response.

The body sends sensations.
modes.ritualCard:
The body sends sensations.
Take one signal—tight chest, warm face, butterflies, restless legs. Pair it with three possible contexts or emotions.
Guess three emotions that could plausibly include the same sensation.
Notice how the sensation itself does not name the feeling. Interoceptive signals are interpreted through context and concepts.

Your brain keeps trying to make the feeling choose a team.

Your brain keeps trying to make the feeling choose a team.

Guess which two opposite-feeling words are both true right now.
Check if complexity becomes easier when contradiction is allowed. Mixed emotions can coexist in the same event.

How this feels now partly depends on where you came from.
modes.ritualCard:
How this feels now partly depends on where you came from.
Take the current experience. Imagine arriving here from a great state, then from a terrible state.
Guess how the same moment would feel after a much better versus much worse preceding hour.
Notice how the same event changes emotional colour through contrast. Affective evaluation is relative to recent reference states.

Current emotion says 'this is forever.'

Guess whether each day genuinely needs the same amount of work, rest, social time, or exercise.

modes.displayName: WOULD YOU DEFEND THE WRONG PICK?
modes.openingLine:
Explanation department can apparently work for either candidate.

Your brain is frighteningly good at explaining choices—even choices it did not make.
modes.ritualCard:
Your brain is frighteningly good at explaining choices—even choices it did not make.
Take two low-stakes near-equal options. Choose one privately, wait a moment, then explain why the other could also be reasonable.
Guess how quickly you could justify a similar option if you forgot which one you originally chose.
Notice how explanation ability is not proof of original preference. People can construct reasons after the fact for choices they did not actually make.

modes.catch: Notice how explanation ability is not proof of original preference.
modes.reveal: People can construct reasons after the fact for choices they did not actually make.
modes.mindBend: A convincing explanation can be generated after the decision, not discovered before it.
modes.moveOn: ↻ WOULD YOU DEFEND THE WRONG PICK?
modes.safety:
PAUSE
Keep the example you picked small, reversible and safe. Do not use momentum as a reason to ignore pain, exhaustion, major consequences or information that needs more thought. Keep the result tied to this one example rather than generalising it to every situation.
modes.returnPrompt: ↻ WOULD YOU DEFEND THE WRONG PICK?
modes.targetPattern: Failing to notice a choice has been switched and then explaining the switched option
modes.mechanismFingerprint: Generate an equally plausible rationale for a non-chosen near-equivalent option to expose how easily reasons can be constructed post hoc.

modes.displayName: RELEASE THE GOAL, KEEP THE VALUE
modes.openingLine:
Route closed. Destination remains on the map.

A goal can become impossible while the value underneath it stays alive.
modes.ritualCard:
A goal can become impossible while the value underneath it stays alive.
Name the blocked goal. Extract the value beneath it—connection, contribution, mastery, security, adventure. Invent one different route to that value.
Guess what the goal was trying to give you at the deepest practical level.
Check if letting go becomes redirection rather than collapse. Adaptive disengagement frees resources when a goal is no longer attainable.

modes.displayName: WHOSE OPINION GOT INTO YOUR POCKET?

Opinion has been checked for borrowed accessories.

People you want connection with can quietly move your opinions.
modes.ritualCard:
People you want connection with can quietly move your opinions.
Take one opinion you hold. Imagine stating it before Person A and Person B. Notice where you soften, strengthen, or reshape it.
Guess which view became easier to express around a particular person.
Catch the social adjustment without calling it fake. People tune attitudes and self-presentation toward relationship-relevant others.

Catch any small automatic echo. People often mimic emotional expressions, which can support shared affect.

modes.displayName: THE OBJECT ISN'T THE WHOLE ERA
modes.openingLine:
Memory has been offered cloud storage.

Sometimes getting rid of a thing feels like deleting a version of you.
modes.ritualCard:
Sometimes getting rid of a thing feels like deleting a version of you.
Name the object, then name the story it represents. Imagine keeping the story in another form—photo, sentence, one smaller item—without keeping the whole object.
Guess what memory or identity the object is carrying.
Check if possession and memory separate slightly. Objects can become extensions of autobiographical identity.

modes.displayName: YOU CHOSE IT; YOU AREN'T IT
modes.openingLine:
Decision has lost its surname.

A decision can become a name tag if you wear it long enough.
modes.ritualCard:
A decision can become a name tag if you wear it long enough.
State the choice without identity grammar: replace 'I'm the kind of person who…' with 'I chose ___ under those conditions.'
Guess how threatening it feels to revise the choice because of what it would 'say about you.'
Check if revision becomes less self-threatening. Choices can fuse with identity and gain protection beyond their current utility.

modes.play: Write the confident wrong answer and the correct answer side by side. Add 1 line explaining exactly why the first one fails.
modes.catch: Notice how surprise makes the correction sticky.
modes.reveal: High-confidence errors can produce strong correction learning.
modes.mindBend: Being confidently wrong can create a memorable update—if you actually update.
modes.safety:
PAUSE
Use the written version as a test, not a verdict. Stop if you begin forcing the result or using it to ignore information that clearly needs action. The result is a working perspective, not proof that the opposite story is true.
modes.targetPattern: High-confidence errors being especially memorable once corrected
modes.mechanismFingerprint: Pair a high-confidence error with immediate corrective feedback and explicit explanation of the violated rule.

modes.openingLine:
Whack-a-mole machine unplugged.

Fighting a memory can turn the session into nothing but memory-monitoring.
modes.ritualCard:
Fighting a memory can turn the session into nothing but memory-monitoring.
For one harmless intrusive memory, replace 'Don’t remember' with 'I notice the memory is available; I'm returning to X.' No checking whether it left.
Guess how often you must check for the memory to know you're successfully 'not thinking' it.
Notice the drop in monitoring work. Intentional suppression requires monitoring for the target and can become effortful or paradoxical.

Doorway charged a tiny memory toll.

You walked into the room and the reason for walking there evaporated.
modes.ritualCard:
You walked into the room and the reason for walking there evaporated.
Next time a harmless intention vanishes after a doorway, mentally reconstruct the previous room, posture, and last action—or physically return if practical.
Guess whether returning to the previous location helps the intention come back.
Check if the old context restores the thought. Event boundaries update working memory and can reduce access to prior goals.

modes.openingLine:
Reminder cue has been removed from six committees.

A reminder attached to everything reminds you of almost nothing.
modes.ritualCard:
A reminder attached to everything reminds you of almost nothing.
Choose one overloaded reminder cue. Replace it with a distinctive cue used for one task only.
Guess whether one generic cue like 'desk' or 'phone' is linked to too many intentions.
Notice how specificity sharpens retrieval. Retrieval cues become less effective when associated with many competing targets.

Memory camera quietly switched to wide-angle.

Your memory can widen the camera after the photo is gone.

Scene memory often extrapolates beyond original boundaries.

MIND BEND
Memory can preserve the world model, not just the captured frame.

MOVE ON

modes.play: Map the last 20 minutes. Identify exercise, rushing, argument, caffeine, excitement, startling news, or stress before the current feeling.
modes.catch: Check if the new emotion inherited an already-revved body.
modes.reveal: Residual physiological arousal can amplify later emotional responses.
modes.mindBend: The second event may not have created all the intensity it received.
modes.safety:
PAUSE
Use this pass to reduce mind-reading, not to manufacture reassurance. Direct communication and boundaries carry more weight than guessed motives. A single pass can test the pattern; it does not need to settle it permanently.
modes.targetPattern: Residual arousal from one event intensifying emotion in the next
modes.mechanismFingerprint: Identify a preceding arousal-producing event and separate residual physiological activation from the current trigger's contribution.

Emotion has submitted a job description.

Two unpleasant feelings can want opposite things from you.
modes.ritualCard:
Two unpleasant feelings can want opposite things from you.
Pick the best functional verb rather than the best emotion word. Name one safe response that fits the function.
Guess whether the state is warning, grieving, protesting, withdrawing, seeking certainty, or seeking connection.
Notice how function can clarify action even when labels stay fuzzy. Emotions organise different action tendencies and concerns.

modes.openingLine:
Mood lost access to one factual spreadsheet cell.

Your mood has more room to colour questions with no clean answer.
modes.ritualCard:
Your mood has more room to colour questions with no clean answer.
Take the current big ambiguous judgment. Break out one factual sub-question that can be answered without mood.
Guess which is more mood-sensitive: 'What time is the meeting?' or 'Is my life going well?'
Notice how certainty improves when the task becomes concrete. Mood influences constructive, open-ended judgments more than simple retrieval.

Brick wall passed inspection. Eyes filed objections.

Straight parallel lines can look tilted when little blocks mess with their edges.
modes.ritualCard:
Straight parallel lines can look tilted when little blocks mess with their edges.
Draw two rows of alternating dark/light squares, offset the second row by half a square, and separate them with a thin grey line.
Guess whether mortar lines stay visually straight between staggered black-and-white tiles.
Notice the line seems to slope despite being straight. Local contrast at staggered edges biases orientation perception.

VIBE: UNFILTERED

Ask who damn wants it before the whole damn group volunteers.

HOOK
A whole group can agree to a plan nobody likes.

PREDICT
Guess what each person would choose if they were guaranteed nobody would be offended.

PLAY
For one low-stakes group decision, ask everyone privately or simultaneously: first choice, second choice, and 'I genuinely don't mind.'

CATCH
Check if public consensus matches private preference.

REVEAL
Groups can coordinate around misperceived preferences.

MIND BEND
Agreement is not proof that anyone wanted the result.

MOVE ON
↻ WHO ACTUALLY WANTS THIS?

Motive detector now works both directions.

Their opinion has motives.

Their opinion has motives.

Guess what self-interest could shape your own interpretation of the same disagreement.

Some relationships run on responsiveness, not perfect accounting.

Take one small exchange. Compare LEDGER MODE—equal repayment now—with COMMUNAL MODE—respond to need over time.
Guess whether you would want a close person to repay this exact favour or simply care when you need them.
Notice which model actually fits the relationship. Communal relationships often organise giving around need rather than immediate equivalence.

modes.play: Choose one emotional public-event memory. Separate verified details from vivid-but-unverified details.
modes.catch: Notice how confidence and source quality can differ.
modes.reveal: Flashbulb memories feel exceptionally vivid and confident but still change over time.
modes.mindBend: A memory can feel photographic without being a photograph.
modes.safety:
PAUSE
Use the chosen example to examine recall, not to force a definitive version of the past. Missing or changing details are allowed to stay uncertain. Leave room for new evidence after the exercise instead of treating the result as final.
modes.targetPattern: Highly emotional public moments feeling photographically accurate despite memory change
modes.mechanismFingerprint: Separate source-verified details from vivid subjective details within an emotional public-event memory.

modes.openingLine:
Old habit may ring the bell twice.

Removing the reward can make a habit briefly try harder.
modes.ritualCard:
Removing the reward can make a habit briefly try harder.
For one harmless habit you are changing, decide in advance what a temporary increase in urge or attempts will mean: 'old learning testing the door.'
Guess whether the urge might spike before it settles when the usual payoff no longer appears.
Check if the spike becomes less surprising. Previously reinforced behaviour can temporarily increase when reinforcement is withdrawn.

Take a sticky checking habit—messages, feeds, scores. Identify whether the payoff is unpredictable rather than constant.

Notice how 'maybe this time' fuels another repetition. Intermittent reinforcement produces persistent responding.

modes.displayName: LET A SMALL GOOD THING HELP THE BODY LAND
modes.openingLine:
Stress stayed true; body found a softer runway.

You do not need to become happy; sometimes a small positive cue helps the body come down.
modes.ritualCard:
You do not need to become happy; sometimes a small positive cue helps the body come down.
After an ordinary stressful moment, spend one minute with something mildly positive and safe—warm interaction, humour, nature, music—without denying the stress.
Guess whether a gentle pleasant stimulus changes recovery speed after mild stress.
Check if breathing, posture, or pace settles. Positive emotions can help undo lingering cardiovascular activation after negative emotion.

Friendship stayed; endless replay lost automatic renewal.

Think of a repeated problem conversation. Mark what is CONNECTION and what is REHEARSAL. Decide whether the next conversation needs comfort, action, or a topic change.

Notice how closeness and rumination can coexist. Co-rumination can strengthen relationships while maintaining negative affect.

modes.displayName: ARE YOU STAYING WORRIED TO AVOID THE DROP?
modes.openingLine:
Worry has been caught selling shock insurance.

Staying tense can feel safer than relaxing and being shocked later.
modes.ritualCard:
Staying tense can feel safer than relaxing and being shocked later.
Imagine two paths: stay worried all day then hear bad news, or have one calm hour then hear the same bad news. Notice which transition you fear more.
Guess whether calm feels risky because bad news would then hit harder.
Catch the preference for steady discomfort over emotional contrast. Some worry is maintained by avoidance of sudden negative emotional shifts.

When something unfair happens, the brain can try to make the world feel orderly by blaming the person.
modes.ritualCard:
When something unfair happens, the brain can try to make the world feel orderly by blaming the person.

Check if moral explanation was appearing faster than causal evidence. Belief in a just world can make random or structural misfortune feel as if it must have been deserved.

modes.openingLine:
Your personal odds have been asked to show receipts.

Average risk applies to everyone—until your brain reaches your own name.
modes.ritualCard:
Average risk applies to everyone—until your brain reaches your own name.
Keep age, situation, habits and information as similar as possible. Compare the two numbers.
Guess your chance of one ordinary negative event, then predict the chance for a genuinely similar person.
Check if 'me' quietly received a discount. People often expect better outcomes for themselves than for comparable others.

modes.displayName: THE FIRST THREE CAN STEER THE CROWD
modes.openingLine:
Crowd may have started as three people and a domino.

A crowd can become confident by copying itself.
modes.ritualCard:
A crowd can become confident by copying itself.
Take a low-stakes rating or option. Write your private answer first, then imagine seeing three people choose the opposite before you respond publicly.
Guess what you would choose if you could not see anyone else's choice.
Notice the pressure to treat their choices as extra evidence. Sequential social choices can create cascades where later people rationally ignore private signals.

modes.displayName: IF THE REWARD WASN'T ENOUGH, WHY DID I DO IT?
modes.openingLine:
Tiny reward forced the mind to write a better story.

When the external excuse is tiny, the mind may rewrite the internal reason.
modes.ritualCard:
When the external excuse is tiny, the mind may rewrite the internal reason.
Imagine doing the same dull activity once for $100 and once for $1. Which version gives you more reason to tell yourself it was okay?
Guess how you explain a boring task after doing it for a huge reward versus a trivial reward.
Catch the need for an internal explanation when the external one is weak. Weak external justification can increase attitude change through dissonance reduction.

modes.displayName: WHAT KIND OF WIN IS THIS?
modes.openingLine:
Goal nutrition label added.

Two ambitious goals can ask for the same effort and feed very different parts of you.
modes.ritualCard:
Two ambitious goals can ask for the same effort and feed very different parts of you.
Take one goal and classify its main payoff. Imagine achieving it privately with nobody impressed.
Guess what the win gives you: status, image, money—or growth, connection, contribution, health.
Notice what value remains after audience effects are removed. Intrinsic and extrinsic aspirations differ in the needs they tend to serve.

modes.play: Cross two adjacent fingers, close your eyes, and gently touch one safe small round object between the crossed fingertips.
modes.catch: Catch the strange sense of two separate objects.
modes.reveal: Your brain interprets touch using the fingers' usual spatial arrangement.
modes.mindBend: The object stayed one; your body map supplied the second.
modes.moveOn: ↻ CROSS YOUR FINGERS, DOUBLE THE OBJECT
modes.safety:
PAUSE
Do this seated at a clear surface. Close your eyes only while still, use a clean blunt object that cannot cut or shatter, keep it away from the face, and stop if you feel dizzy or your fingers hurt or go numb.
modes.returnPrompt: ↻ CROSS YOUR FINGERS, DOUBLE THE OBJECT
modes.targetPattern: One object touched with crossed fingers feeling like two objects
modes.theoryBackbone: Aristotle illusion; tactile perception; body maps
modes.mechanismFingerprint: Cross adjacent fingers so one physical object stimulates skin locations normally contacted by two separate objects, producing a doubled tactile percept.

modes.ritualCard:
A circle can change size without changing a millimetre.
Draw two equal centre circles. Put a close-fitting outer ring around one and a much larger ring around the other. Compare, then measure.
Guess which identical centre circle looks larger: one inside a tight ring or one inside a huge ring.
Notice the centre circles appear unequal. Size judgments are influenced by surrounding scale.

modes.openingLine:
Tiny border somehow got a whole wall-painting contract.

A tiny boundary can make entire regions look lighter or darker.
modes.ritualCard:
A tiny boundary can make entire regions look lighter or darker.
Imagine two equal grey panels touching, with a narrow bright strip on one side of the border and dark strip on the other. Cover the edge mentally or physically.
Guess whether two broad grey areas with equal centres can look different if their shared edge has a light-dark gradient.
Catch the large-area brightness difference collapse when the edge disappears. The visual system infers surface brightness strongly from local edge structure.

Colour can seem to seep from a line into empty space.
modes.ritualCard:
Colour can seem to seep from a line into empty space.
Draw a closed wavy shape using a darker outer line and a lighter coloured inner line. Leave the inside white.
Guess whether a pale region appears filled when bordered by two thin contrasting coloured contours.
Check if the interior takes on a faint wash of the inner colour. Contour interactions can create long-range colour filling-in.

modes.displayName: THE OBJECT WORKS UNTIL YOU LOOK AT ALL OF IT
modes.openingLine:
Every department passed inspection; company is physically impossible.

Every small piece makes sense.
modes.ritualCard:
Every small piece makes sense.
Draw or picture the classic blivet: three round prongs at one end blending into two rectangular bars at the other. Trace each edge slowly.
Guess whether you can follow each prong of an impossible trident from one end to the other without contradiction.
Catch the point where local geometry stops agreeing globally. The visual system prioritises locally coherent interpretations even when they cannot coexist.

modes.displayName: YOUR BRAIN REFUSES THE INSIDE-OUT FACE
modes.openingLine:
Face prior has overruled geometry.

Faces are so familiar your brain may choose the wrong depth rather than accept an inside-out one.
modes.ritualCard:
Faces are so familiar your brain may choose the wrong depth rather than accept an inside-out one.
Imagine a thin face mask turned concave toward you. Picture moving side to side while the nose seems to follow.
Guess whether a hollow mask viewed from the inside would still look like a normal outward face.
Catch expectation overpowering geometry. Strong face priors can dominate weaker depth cues.

modes.openingLine:
Wheel went forward; perception filed reverse gear.

Continuous forward motion can look backward when your visual samples land at the wrong rhythm.
modes.ritualCard:
Continuous forward motion can look backward when your visual samples land at the wrong rhythm.
Imagine a wheel rotating slightly less than one spoke spacing between snapshots. Track which spoke your brain matches across frames.
Guess how a spoke wheel might appear under flickering light or video when each new frame resembles an earlier spoke position.
Catch apparent reversal emerge from matching. Discrete temporal sampling can create aliasing in motion perception.

modes.reveal: People often overestimate their share of collaborative work because their own contributions are more accessible in memory.
modes.mindBend: What is easiest to remember can look like what mattered most.

modes.openingLine:
Compliment survived quality assurance.

A genuine compliment can feel socially enormous right before you say it.
modes.ritualCard:
A genuine compliment can feel socially enormous right before you say it.
Choose one concrete, non-intrusive compliment about effort, taste, skill, kindness, or contribution. Imagine receiving it first.

modes.displayName: LOOK AT THE SAME THING TOGETHER
modes.openingLine:
Connection found a third object to stand on.

Connection can happen sideways—through a shared object, joke, view, problem, or moment.
modes.ritualCard:
Connection can happen sideways—through a shared object, joke, view, problem, or moment.
With someone safe, direct attention to one shared external experience and exchange one reaction each.
Guess whether talking face-to-face about yourselves feels different from jointly noticing the same external thing.
Notice the 'we saw that' feeling. Shared reality develops when people experience an inner state as common toward the same external target.

modes.displayName: WHY DOES THEIR WIN STING HERE?
modes.openingLine:
Jealousy just pointed to the part of the résumé you care about.

The same friend's success can feel inspiring in one area and irritating in another.
modes.ritualCard:
The same friend's success can feel inspiring in one area and irritating in another.
Imagine the same person succeeding spectacularly in a domain you genuinely Don’t care about. Compare the emotional reaction.
Guess which ingredient makes this comparison sting: closeness, their success, or how central the domain is to you.
Notice the threat shrink when self-relevance disappears. Comparison threat depends strongly on how important the domain is to one's own self-evaluation.

modes.displayName: WHAT IF THIS IS ONE OF THE LAST TEN?
modes.openingLine:
Routine has received a limited-edition label.

Ordinary things become visible when an ending appears.
modes.ritualCard:
Ordinary things become visible when an ending appears.
Choose something benign and recurring—a school pickup, route, lunch place, team ritual, child's bedtime story. Imagine only ten remain.
Guess how differently you would notice this routine if you knew you had only ten more of them.
Notice which details suddenly matter. Perceived endings increase attention and appreciation of familiar experiences.

Experience has received two review categories.

Some valuable experiences are satisfying in retrospect and annoying in minute seven.
modes.ritualCard:
Some valuable experiences are satisfying in retrospect and annoying in minute seven.
Take one effortful valued activity. Rate PLEASURE DURING and WORTH AFTER separately.
Guess whether the activity is meant to feel pleasant now or meaningful afterward.
Check if one low number had been cancelling the other dimension. Pleasure and meaning are related but distinct components of wellbeing.

modes.displayName: THE CHOICE STARTS EDITING THE OPTIONS
modes.openingLine:
Decision has been caught editing the contestants after voting closed.

Once you choose, your brain may help you live with it by moving the ratings apart.
modes.ritualCard:
Once you choose, your brain may help you live with it by moving the ratings apart.
For a recent close choice, reconstruct the pre-choice pros of the rejected option and cons of the chosen one before reading your current story.
Guess how you rated the winner and runner-up before the decision.
Check if the alternatives have drifted apart after commitment. Post-decision dissonance can increase liking of chosen options and decrease liking of rejected ones.

modes.displayName: ASKING CAN LOOK SMARTER THAN PRETENDING
modes.openingLine:
Competence has discovered delegation.

You may think asking advice announces incompetence.
modes.ritualCard:
You may think asking advice announces incompetence.
Rewrite 'I don't know what I'm doing' as one bounded advice request: 'You've handled X—what would you watch for here?'
Guess how you view someone who asks you a specific question in an area you know well.
Notice the difference between helplessness and selective advice-seeking. People often view advice seekers more favourably, especially when their expertise is acknowledged.

Notice how support becomes targeted instead of generic. Social support is more effective when it matches the stressor and recipient's needs.

modes.openingLine:
Support response has acquired three signal bars.

People often remember whether they felt understood before they remember your brilliant advice.
modes.ritualCard:
People often remember whether they felt understood before they remember your brilliant advice.
In one supportive reply, include one line for each needed signal: 'I hear X,' 'that makes sense because Y,' 'I'm with you / what would help?'
Guess which signal is missing: understood, validated, cared for.
Notice how the response feels different from jumping to solutions. Perceived responsiveness is central to intimacy and relationship wellbeing.

The more facts you hang from one hook, the longer it can take to grab the right one.
modes.ritualCard:
The more facts you hang from one hook, the longer it can take to grab the right one.
Choose one overloaded topic in your notes. Split its facts into smaller labelled subgroups instead of one giant heading.
Guess which answer comes faster: a person linked to one location or a person linked to five locations.
Notice how retrieval gains narrower routes. Retrieval slows when a cue fans out to many competing associations.

Old learning left invisible scaffolding.

You may not be able to perform it now, yet your brain can still have invisible leftovers.

You may not be able to perform it now, yet your brain can still have invisible leftovers.
Return to one harmless old skill, word set, route, or procedure. Compare how quickly familiarity and performance return versus the original learning period.

Notice hidden learning reveal itself through speed. Prior learning can survive as savings even when unaided recall or performance is poor.

Brain remembered the search route and outsourced the cargo.

When the internet promises to remember it, your brain may remember the route instead.

When the internet promises to remember it, your brain may remember the route instead.
Take one useful fact you normally bookmark. Before saving it, retrieve it once from memory and then save the source.
Guess whether you retain the fact itself or mostly where you could find it again.
Notice the difference between content memory and location memory. People allocate memory differently when information is expected to remain externally available.

modes.displayName: THE NOTE HELPS — AND LETS MEMORY RELAX
modes.openingLine:
Checklist did its job so well memory clocked off.

A reminder can make you better at the task and worse at remembering the reminder's contents.
modes.ritualCard:
A reminder can make you better at the task and worse at remembering the reminder's contents.
For one harmless item, compare using an external checklist with trying to reconstruct it afterward without looking.
Guess what you would recall if the note disappeared after you relied on it all day.
Notice what performance gained and memory delegated. Offloading reduces cognitive demand but can reduce internal encoding.

Future-you has excellent principles from a safe distance.

From Tuesday, Friday-you is very disciplined.

From Tuesday, Friday-you is very disciplined.

Ordinary behaviour just became currency.

A behaviour you normally do freely can become rewarding when access is briefly restricted.

A behaviour you normally do freely can become rewarding when access is briefly restricted.
Choose a harmless frequent behaviour and reserve it until after a small target action. Keep the restriction mild and voluntary.
Guess whether ten minutes of a favourite ordinary activity feels more valuable after you cannot do it during a work block.
Notice how ordinary access becomes incentive. Restricting a high-frequency behaviour below its preferred level can make access to it reinforcing.

A racing system can be read as 'I'm failing' or 'my body is mobilising.'

A racing system can be read as 'I'm failing' or 'my body is mobilising.'
Take one safe stress cue—alertness, faster heart, energy. Write DEBILITATING STORY and MOBILISING STORY without pretending the sensation is pleasant.

modes.displayName: CAN'T CHANGE IT OR HAVEN'T TESTED A LEVER?
modes.openingLine:
Whole emotion stayed employed; one department changed.

The sentence 'nothing helps' can shut down experiments before they start.
modes.ritualCard:
The sentence 'nothing helps' can shut down experiments before they start.
Choose one lever only: body arousal, attention, interpretation, environment, action urge, social contact. Test it for two minutes.
Guess one part of the state you might influence without controlling the whole emotion.
Check if any component moves even if the emotion stays. Beliefs about regulation capacity influence strategy use and persistence.

modes.displayName: PUT ORDINARY TUESDAY BACK IN THE FUTURE
modes.openingLine:
Future event has been forced to share the calendar with laundry.

Your forecast contains the event in HD and everyday life in invisible ink.
modes.ritualCard:
Your forecast contains the event in HD and everyday life in invisible ink.
Keep the future event exactly as imagined. Add five ordinary activities that will coexist with it afterward.
Guess what you will actually be doing three days after the outcome: breakfast, messages, work, errands, people, sleep.
Notice how the emotional future gains competing inputs. Affective forecasts often underrepresent adaptation and the return of ordinary attention demands.
